name: Meradimate

lead: Meradimate (menthyl anthranilate) is a UVA filter used to add UVA coverage in sunscreens, helping protect skin from the sun damage that drives photoaging.

It absorbs UVA light and has been characterised as fluorescent, with studies mapping its excited-state behaviour. It is one of the 17 ingredients the FDA lists for OTC sunscreens. Research on it is mainly photophysical and in vitro; no clinical outcome trials were found.

paras: It is used in some products alongside other filters, for example a US sports sunscreen listing it with octinoxate, octisalate and oxybenzone. It works as part of a combined filter system in daily or outdoor SPF.
Labels advise stopping use if rash occurs. Lab studies have examined cell effects and sperm-signalling interactions of UV filters; no clinical outcome data were found.

angle.text: Meradimate is an older anthranilate UVA filter listed in US sunscreen rules, used to add UVA coverage that helps protect skin from sun aging. It has been studied mostly for its photophysics rather than for appearance outcomes.

lead: Meradimate (menthyl anthranilate) is an ester of anthranilic acid and menthol that acts as a UVA filter in sunscreens [1]. It is one of the 17 ingredients the US FDA lists for over-the-counter sunscreen products [1]. It should not be confused with methyl anthranilate [1].
Published research on it is mostly photophysical. A US label for a sports sunscreen lists it with octinoxate, octisalate and oxybenzone [2].

paras: Studies report that menthyl anthranilate is strongly fluorescent in ethanol and characterise its excited states [3][4]. Work on the related methyl anthranilate examined its photoprotection mechanism [5], and another study found antioxidants suppressed singlet-oxygen generation sensitised by menthyl anthranilate [6].

In cell studies chemical filters showed contradictory effects in UV/ROS-stressed keratinocytes and fibroblasts [7]. A study of UV filters and human sperm found several filters mimicked progesterone-like calcium signalling through CatSper channels [8]. These are laboratory findings, not clinical outcomes.

A DailyMed sunscreen label listing meradimate states that it helps prevent sunburn and, with other sun protection measures, decreases the risk of skin cancer and early skin aging; it warns users to stop use and ask a doctor if rash occurs [2].
